The first factory workers

In the 1830s and 1840s, textile mills in Lowell, Massachusetts hired thousands of young women from New England farms. Their letters and newspapers are among the richest sources we have on early industrial work.

This week: read a mill worker's letter and analyze it as historical evidence.

Over the unit we follow industrialization from those first mills to the giant steel and railroad corporations of the 1890s. You will read the words of a mill worker, a steel magnate, and a farmers' political party, and decide for yourself: did industrialization expand opportunity for American workers, or did it mainly concentrate wealth and power?

Historians ask four questions of every source: Who made it, when and why (sourcing)? What was happening at the time (context)? What does it show, and what is my claim about it (claim and evidence)? Do other sources agree (corroboration)? You will use these four questions all semester.

Key terms: wage labor, piece rate, boardinghouse, strike, labor union, trust, monopoly, Populist.
title: Voices from the Mills
